paragraphs.heading: The midnight zone
paragraphs.text: The bathypelagic zone is the stretch of open ocean from 1,000 to 4,000 m below the surface. Its name comes from the Greek word for deep. It sits under the mesopelagic zone and above the abyssopelagic zone. People also call it the midnight zone, since no sunlight gets down this far.

paragraphs.heading: Cold, dark and crushing
paragraphs.text: Conditions here barely change: the water stays at about 4 °C, and its saltiness runs from 33 to 35 g/kg. There is almost no light, and even light made by living things is scarce. Water pressure rises by 1 atmosphere for each 10 m of depth, so here it reaches 100 to 400 atmospheres. Scientists think these conditions have held steady for the last 8000 years.

paragraphs.heading: Food falling from above
paragraphs.text: With no sunlight, nothing here can grow by photosynthesis, so there are no phytoplankton or water plants. Instead, most food arrives from the layers above as particulate organic matter, or POM, carried down in copepod droppings and dead organisms. These drifting scraps are nicknamed marine snow or ocean dandruff, and they bring carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus down to the animals below the sunlit layer. Animals eat some of the POM on the way down, but small pieces often clump together, sink faster and are more likely to reach these depths.

paragraphs.heading: Life around hot vents
paragraphs.text: In some parts of the zone there are hydrothermal vents, which form mostly where Earth's tectonic plates pull apart at mid-ocean ridges. The vents give off heat and chemicals such as sulfide and methane. Some communities use these chemicals instead of sunlight as their energy source, a process called chemoautotrophy. The vents also leave minerals on the seafloor, which makes them a target of interest for deep-sea mining.

paragraphs.heading: Where calcite dissolves
paragraphs.text: Near the bottom of the zone, at about 3,500 m, lies the lysocline: the depth at which calcite starts to dissolve quickly, though it varies between ocean basins. Deeper, colder water under more pressure dissolves more calcium carbonate, so less of it survives the trip to the seafloor. Because dissolving speeds up so sharply here, the seafloor mud of this zone holds very different amounts of calcium carbonate from place to place.

paragraphs.heading: Still a mystery
paragraphs.text: The zone is bigger by volume than the sunlit photic zone, yet we know little about it. Collecting samples from such depths is hard and costly, and measuring microbes under such pressure is a technical challenge of its own. One open question is how fast microbes here break down carbon, since past studies gave rates much higher than expected. Answering it may change how scientists understand Earth's carbon cycle.
